memory_update.text: PAR is a high-priority underfollowed candidate for the restaurant delivery/ordering/loyalty/customer-data stack because it combines POS, loyalty, engagement, ordering, and restaurant operations software with small-cap market size.

NCR Voyix is a plausible underfollowed second-order candidate after its restructuring because its Restaurants segment includes POS, ordering, payments, loyalty/data, and managed services, but evidence must separate recurring software quality from legacy hardware and debt risk.
Toast is the scaled public reference for restaurant operating-system consolidation, but its market cap and investor awareness make it less suitable as the main underfollowed alpha lane.

The most relevant chokepoint signals are not delivery order volume alone; they are active restaurant locations, loyalty members, GPV/payment volume, ordering module attach, data/analytics adoption, and evidence that restaurants use the platform to own repeat customer behavior.

Olo was formerly one of the cleanest pure-play public ordering platforms, but its 2025 Thoma Bravo acquisition removes it from the active US-listed universe; later layers should search for remaining public substitutes such as payments/POS vendors, reservation platforms inside larger companies, and restaurant-specific loyalty vendors.
PAR should be retained for deeper Layer 2 work as the cleanest small-cap public mapping to restaurant POS, loyalty, ordering, payments, and analytics infrastructure.

VYX should be tracked as a small-cap turnaround-style restaurant commerce infrastructure candidate; the key risk is whether restaurant software growth is offset by legacy complexity, debt, or restructuring noise.
FOUR is a plausible second-order payments infrastructure candidate, but restaurant-specific exposure must be verified before it can rank above purer restaurant-tech names.

Olo was once a strong public pure-play for restaurant ordering and guest-data infrastructure, but it was taken private by Thoma Bravo in September 2025 and should be used only as a private benchmark or M&A signal.

The likely chokepoint within restaurant delivery and loyalty is the system-of-record layer that unifies POS events, ordering origin, payments, loyalty identity, menu pricing, promotions, and guest data across first-party and marketplace channels.

Olo was the cleanest pure-play public restaurant ordering/customer-data platform, but it ceased trading after the September 12, 2025 Thoma Bravo acquisition; public exposure must now be proxied through POS, payments, loyalty, and restaurant-operations platforms.

PAR should be prioritized for later Serenity layers because it has unusually direct node exposure across loyalty, ordering, POS, payments, and back-office restaurant software while remaining below the typical large-cap attention threshold.
NCR Voyix may be misclassified by the market as legacy retail/POS infrastructure; after divestitures, restaurant ARR and Aloha Next SaaS migration are key hidden signals.

Shift4's restaurant relevance depends on whether SkyTab and Lighthouse attach to payments in a way that captures ordering, customer engagement, loyalty, and transaction-level data rather than remaining a generic payments processor.

Several relevant restaurant loyalty/order orchestration vendors appear private, acquired, or embedded inside larger payment companies; later passes should check private-vendor displacement risk for PAR, VYX, FOUR, and TOST.

PAR Technology is a high-priority underfollowed candidate for the restaurant ordering, loyalty, POS, and customer-data stack because restaurant technology is core to its product portfolio and market cap is within the preferred discovery range.

NCR Voyix is a messy but relevant underfollowed candidate after divesting digital banking; Restaurant segment exposure through Aloha/Voyix POS, payments, ordering, and fulfillment should be tracked separately from legacy retail/hardware noise.
Toast should remain the reference leader for restaurant POS/payments/software but should not crowd out smaller infrastructure candidates in this node.

Olo would have been one of the cleanest pure-play public candidates, but it is no longer US-listed after Thoma Bravo completed the acquisition on 2025-09-12; use it as a private-company benchmark only.

Need a follow-up pass on public payments processors and restaurant-adjacent platforms such as Shift4, Fiserv/Clover, Global Payments/Heartland, and Block/Square to separate true restaurant-data exposure from generic merchant-acquiring exposure.

node: Delivery, ordering, loyalty, and customer-data stack
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expands the public-company universe around restaurant delivery, ordering, loyalty, POS, payments, and customer-data control. The reference lane is anchored by DoorDash as the scaled third-party marketplace and Toast as the scaled restaurant operating system/POS platform. The underfollowed lane highlights PAR Technology and NCR Voyix, both more niche restaurant-tech infrastructure names with direct exposure to enterprise restaurant POS, loyalty, ordering, payments, and data workflows. Olo would have been a strong pure-play ordering candidate, but it was acquired by Thoma Bravo and delisted in 2025, so it is excluded from the active US-listed candidate set. Layer 1B expansion for the restaurant delivery, ordering, loyalty, and customer-data stack finds one large reference platform and three smaller or less obvious infrastructure suppliers. The most relevant underfollowed lane is not delivery marketplaces themselves, but POS, loyalty, ordering, payments, and commerce-platform vendors embedded inside restaurant operating systems. Olo would have been a highly relevant public pure-play, but it completed a take-private transaction in September 2025 and should be tracked only as a private benchmark, not a current US-listed candidate. Expanded the universe around restaurant-owned digital ordering, POS, loyalty, payments, and guest-data infrastructure. The most direct public pure-play, Olo, is no longer US-listed after Thoma Bravo completed its acquisition in September 2025, which creates a public-market coverage gap.
